stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = 7 \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 4 < c < 10 \), such that \( f'(c) = -3 \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(10) - f(4)}{10 - 4} = -3 \), f is not differentiable at \( x = 7 \), which lies in \( (4, 10) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[4, 10\right] \) is \( \frac{f(10) - f(4)}{10 - 4} = \frac{2 - 20}{6} = -3 \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[4, 10\right] \) and differentiable on \( (4, 10) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = 7 \), which lies in \( (4, 10) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = -3 \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem
